content.page_summary: Recommendations on invasive strategies for acute coronary syndromes, focusing on timing and indications for CABG, PCI, and angiography in STEMI and NSTE-ACS patients.
content.5.2.1_emergency_CABG: Emergency coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) should be considered for patients with a patent infarct-related artery (IRA) but unsuitable anatomy for PCI, and either a large myocardial area at jeopardy or with cardiogenic shock (CS). CABG is recommended at the time of surgical repair for MI-related mechanical complications requiring coronary revascularization. In STEMI patients with failed PCI or acute coronary occlusion not amenable to PCI, emergency CABG is infrequently performed because benefits are less certain and delay to reperfusion reduces probability of myocardial salvage; surgical risks may be elevated.
content.5.2.1.1_invasive_strategy_in_STEMI_late_: Routine immediate angiography and PCI (if indicated) clearly benefit patients presenting within 12 h of symptom onset. For STEMI patients presenting later than 12 h, the value of routine PPCI is less well established. A small RCT (n=347) of patients presenting 12–48 h after symptom onset without persistent symptoms reported improved myocardial salvage and long-term survival with a routine PPCI strategy. Observational data from FAST-MI showed lower all-cause death at 1 month and at median follow-up with an invasive strategy. However, in stable patients with persistent occlusion of the IRA 3–28 days after MI, the Occluded Artery Trial (OAT, n=2166) reported no clinical benefit from routine coronary intervention versus medical management; a meta-analysis also showed no benefit of late recanalization. Therefore, routine PCI of an occluded IRA in STEMI patients presenting >48 h after symptom onset without persistent symptoms is not indicated; manage these patients similarly to chronic total occlusion per ESC chronic coronary syndrome guidelines.
content.evidence_and_references: Small RCT (n=347) referenced; FAST-MI nationwide observational studies; OAT (n=2166) referenced; meta-analysis cited. Reference numbers shown in text (e.g., 185,187,188,189,190,191,192,193,194,195) indicate guideline citations.
content.5.2.2_immediate_invasive_strategy_for_NS: An immediate invasive strategy refers to emergency (as soon as possible) angiography and PCI if indicated. Recommended for patients with working diagnosis of NSTE-ACS and any of the following very high–risk criteria: haemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock; recurrent or ongoing chest pain refractory to medical treatment; acute heart failure presumed secondary to ongoing myocardial ischemia.
